newsitem.title: USA: Smoke trial judge bars testimony on missing Reynolds letter.
newsitem.headline: Smoke trial judge bars testimony on missing Reynolds letter.

text.p: The judge in a $5 billion secondhand-smoke trial on Thursday barred testimony about a missing letter that purportedly suggested an R.J. Reynolds Tobacco executive tried to pressure former President Nixon into firing a surgeon general because of his tobacco stance.
The ruling was made by Judge Robert Kaye of Dade County Court regarding testimony by the former surgeon general, Jesse Steinfeld.

According to lawyers representing 60,000 non-smoking flight attendants suing U.S. cigarette companies, Steinfeld was given the Reynolds letter in October, 1972, to draft a response. The letter, plaintiffs lawyer Stanley Rosenblatt said, reminded Nixon of Reynolds' cash contributions to his re-election campaign and a verbal promise to fire Steinfeld.
It was written shortly before Nixon's landslide re-election, the lawyers said.

Steinfeld, the first surgeon general to propose limits on smoking in public places out of fears secondhand smoke was injuring non-smokers, was asked to resign shortly after the election in November, 1972, Rosenblatt said.

However, rival lawyers said Steinfeld was unable to locate his own copy of the Reynolds letter; a search of Nixon's archives had proven fruitless; and Reynolds was unable to find a copy of the letter.
"This is total hearsay ... hearsay upon hearsay," said Hugh Whiting, an attorney for Reynolds, urging to forbid testimony on the missing letter.

Kaye said the letter's existence could not be sufficiently proven. But he allowed Rosenblatt to question Steinfeld about other government memoranda and letters referring to the missing Reynolds letter.
